issues.legal_issue: Execution of a joint decree for possession is restricted when the judgment debtor acquires an undivided interest from a coparcener and the interests in the property remain unascertained.
material_facts: A decree for actual possession had been passed in favour of members of a joint family.
The judgment debtor claimed to have acquired an undivided interest in the property from some coparceners who were decree holders.
The judgment debtor was already in possession, and the interests of the coparceners in the property were undefined and disputed.
issues.conclusion: The decree could not be executed to dispossess the judgment debtor before the relevant rights were ascertained. The decree was extinguished to the extent of the interest transferred, and the rights had to be worked out through an appropriate partition suit where the shares could not be determined in execution.
issues.legal_principle: A decree in favour of a joint family is treated as a joint decree. Under Section 47 and Order XXI Rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a joint decree may be executed as a whole, but execution in part is possible only when the decree holders’ shares are defined, ascertainable, or undisputed. A transfer of a coparcener’s interest to the judgment debtor extinguishes the decree to that extent. Where the shares are undefined and the judgment debtor is already in possession, the executing court cannot determine the shares or deprive the judgment debtor of possession before the rights are appropriately ascertained, ordinarily in a partition suit. The Court stated that the cited authorities did not detract from this principle, without discussing them individually.

rule.if: execution_of_joint_possession_decree and decree_benefits_joint_family and judgment_debtor_acquired_coparcener_interest and coparcener_shares_undefined_or_disputed and judgment_debtor_already_in_possession

predicates.execution_of_joint_possession_decree: A court is asked to execute a decree requiring possession of immovable property.
predicates.decree_benefits_joint_family: The decree for possession benefits members of a joint family collectively.
predicates.judgment_debtor_acquired_coparcener_inte: The judgment debtor acquired an interest in the property from one or more coparceners who benefit from the decree.
predicates.coparcener_shares_undefined_or_disputed: The coparceners’ interests in the property have not been specifically ascertained or are disputed.
predicates.judgment_debtor_already_in_possession: The judgment debtor is already in possession of the property.

issues.definition: When execution of a joint family possession decree is sought in these circumstances, the current possessor cannot be dispossessed before the relevant shares are ascertained.

issues.legal_issue: The rule requiring a tenant to surrender possession and pursue separately a title acquired after the decree does not apply to an occupant adjudged to be a trespasser rather than a tenant.
material_facts: The occupant had asserted that he was a tenant, but a prior finding in the litigation held that he was a trespasser and not a tenant.
In execution, the occupant claimed to have acquired an undivided interest in the property from coparceners of the decree holder’s family.
The appellants relied on the rule discussed in Sant Lal Jain v. Avtar Singh to argue that the occupant had to surrender possession and pursue any later-acquired title separately.
issues.conclusion: The rule in Sant Lal Jain did not assist the appellants because the occupant was held to be a trespasser, not a lessee. The Court did not examine the scope of Section 111(d) of the Transfer of Property Act because the occupant was not a lessee.
issues.legal_principle: Sant Lal Jain v. Avtar Singh, 1985 (2) SCC 332, explains that a tenant cannot set up title in himself during the tenancy or in proceedings for possession after termination of the tenancy, and generally must surrender possession and pursue separately a title acquired later through another person. The decision also recognizes that separate pursuit is unnecessary where title is acquired from the lessor or someone claiming through the lessor, in which event merger may arise. The Court distinguished that rule because the occupant here had been held to be a trespasser, not a lessee; it expressly left the scope of Section 111(d) of the Transfer of Property Act unexamined.

predicates.ejectment_decree_execution_dispute: The dispute arises in execution of a decree for possession following an ejectment action.
predicates.occupant_adjudged_not_to_be_tenant: The occupant was adjudged in the proceedings to be a trespasser rather than a tenant.
predicates.occupant_claims_acquired_property_title: The occupant claims to have acquired a property interest after the proceedings giving rise to the possession decree.

issues.definition: The tenant’s duty to surrender possession before pursuing a later-acquired title does not bar the title claim when the occupant was adjudged not to be a tenant.
